analysis.one_liner: Designates millions of acres of Utah red rock canyons as protected wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill won 94 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently protect a large network of federal lands in southern and western Utah — the red rock canyon country of the Colorado Plateau and the desert ranges of the Great Basin — by adding them to the National Wilderness Preservation System. Wilderness designation bars new mining, oil and gas leasing, and permanent road building on the land, while continuing existing livestock grazing and protecting traditional uses like hunting, fishing, and hiking. It also reserves federal water rights for the wilderness areas and protects tribal rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who use public land — hikers, hunters, anglers, rafters, campers, and photographers — get permanent access to some of the last large unprotected wild landscapes in the continental United States. The bill's own findings point to climate and wildlife benefits, and it explicitly protects places of Indigenous cultural and ceremonial use.

how_it_helps.text: Designates wilderness across nine Utah regions — including the San Rafael Swell, Canyonlands Basin, Book Cliffs, and Glen Canyon areas — for the benefit and enjoyment of present and future generations.
Withdraws the designated lands from mineral and geothermal leasing, mining claims, and other disposal under public land laws, locking in public access rather than private extraction.
Reserves federal water rights for each wilderness area with a priority date of enactment, protecting flows in desert rivers and streams that the public uses for recreation and that sustain wildlife.
Protects hunting, fishing, hiking, camping, and Indigenous cultural and ceremonial uses of the land, and states that nothing in the bill affects tribal rights.

The bill's findings describe the land as one of the largest remaining unprotected wild expanses in the continental U.S. and cite climate benefits from limiting surface disturbance and fossil fuel extraction.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, mining, and geothermal companies lose access to federal minerals on the designated lands, and off-road vehicle users lose motorized routes inside wilderness boundaries. Utah state and local governments also give up potential future revenue from development on these federal lands, though existing grazing permits continue unchanged.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy and mining firms, off-road users

drawbacks.text: The designation permanently closes the designated lands to future energy and mineral development, which Utah officials and the state's congressional delegation have long argued costs the state economic activity and local revenue.
Wilderness rules restrict new road construction and motorized travel inside the boundaries, a real cost for off-road recreation users and for any future access needs.

The bill reserves federal water rights in Utah, which the state's water users could see as complicating existing state water-law priorities, even though the bill states it does not affect prior federal water rights and creates no precedent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades one-time and ongoing resource extraction on a defined stretch of federal land for permanent public access and conservation of one of the country's largest unprotected wild landscapes. The costs fall on a concentrated set of extractive industries and motorized users; the benefits are broadly shared but diffuse, and largely accrue over decades. Existing grazing and valid existing rights are preserved, which narrows the economic disruption. The main honest objection is that the designation forecloses options forever, including for future generations of Utahns who might weigh development differently.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its public lands subcommittee, never received a markup or floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Lowenthal introduced the bill on June 8, 2021, with 94 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the day it was introduced, and a month later to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands.
No further action was ever taken; the bill was never voted on in committee or on the House floor before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, mining, and geothermal interests are better off because the bill died: the lands remain open to leasing and claims, and off-road users keep current motorized access. Utah officials retain full say over the land's future rather than a permanent federal wilderness designation.

for.name: Rep. Alan Lowenthal
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the America's Red Rock Wilderness Act and recruited 94 original cosponsors.

for.name: Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance
for.what_they_did: Longtime lead advocacy organization pushing Congress to pass the Red Rock wilderness bill.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee and its public lands subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat at the subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Utah's congressional delegation
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Red Rock wilderness bill, as they have across multiple Congresses, arguing it locks up Utah land from development.

sides.party_line_note: All 94 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill also never advanced in the committee process.

industries.note: The bill withdraws the designated lands from all mineral and geothermal leasing, ending the industry's access to potential drilling on this public land. Their gain under the status quo comes at the cost of the public's access to and enjoyment of the same land.
New mining claims and patents are barred on the designated lands, closing a frontier for prospecting and development.
Wilderness designation restricts motorized routes inside the boundaries, shrinking the open area available for off-road use around Moab and elsewhere.
Grazing authorized as of enactment continues within the wilderness areas under reasonable regulation, so ranchers lose nothing under the bill.
